procedural_history.originating_court: Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the High Court dismissing in limine the appeal of four appellants while admitting the appeal of a co-accused (Kondu) for hearing on the merits after notice to the State.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The four appellants and Kondu were jointly tried and convicted. They jointly appealed to the High Court of Bombay. The High Court (Chandurkar, J.) admitted the appeal of Kondu but dismissed the appeal of the four appellants in limine.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The four appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's order dismissing their appeal in limine while admitting the co-accused's appeal. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and remanded the case back to the High Court for a hearing on the merits of all appeals together.

directions: The order dismissing in limine the appeal of the four appellants before us is set aside.
The case is sent back to the High Court for hearing their appeal with the record after giving notice to the State, along with the appeal of Kondo, accused.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the appeal of four co-accused in limine, while simultaneously admitting the appeal of another co-accused in the same case, especially when the cases were interconnected.

facts: Four appellants and another co-accused, K, were jointly tried and convicted for offences including rioting under s. 147 IPC.
All five individuals filed a single, joint memorandum of appeal to the High Court.
The High Court admitted the appeal for co-accused K, but dismissed the appeal for the four appellants 'in limine' (at the threshold, without a full hearing).
law: Under s. 421 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a High Court has the power to dismiss an appeal in limine.
However, this power should not be exercised when an appeal raises a serious, substantial, and prima facie arguable point.

In such cases, it is improper for the High Court to dismiss the appeal summarily, especially without providing reasons, as this deprives the Supreme Court of the High Court's opinion on the matter in a subsequent appeal.
application: The Supreme Court found that the cases of all five accused were interconnected, particularly because the charge of rioting under s. 147 IPC required proving the existence of an 'unlawful assembly,' which inherently links all participants.
The defense raised by K (that the victim was injured by falling on a stone), if successful, would also require serious consideration for the other four appellants.
The very fact that the High Court admitted K's appeal indicated that there was an arguable point in the case.

Given the interconnected nature of the charges and the presence of an arguable point applicable to all, the Court determined it was an "eminently fit case" to admit the appeal for all five accused so their cases could be considered together on the merits.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's order dismissing the appeal of the four appellants in limine was insupportable and unjustified. It allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's dismissal order, and sent the case back to the High Court to hear the appeal of the four appellants on its merits, along with the pending appeal of the co-accused K.

issue.issue_text: Whether a High Court, when summarily dismissing a criminal appeal that raises serious and arguable points, has a duty to provide reasons or some indication of its views on the points raised.

facts: Four appellants, who were convicted along with a co-accused (K), filed a joint appeal in the High Court.
The High Court admitted the appeal for the co-accused (K) but summarily dismissed the appeal for the four appellants with a one-word order: "rejected".
The Supreme Court found that the appeal raised "serious and substantial point[s] which is prima facie arguable."
law: Under Section 421 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a High Court has the power to dismiss an appeal summarily (in limine) after perusing the appeal petition and hearing the appellant.
A summary dismissal is a judicial decision that vitally affects the convicted appellant.
Citing several precedents, the Court affirmed the principle that High Courts should not summarily reject criminal appeals that raise arguable and substantial points.
application: The Court reasoned that an order simply stating "rejected" is "inscrutable" and "does not speak," making it nearly impossible to detect errors.
Such an order is problematic because it deprives the Supreme Court of the High Court's views on the arguable points, which is necessary for a proper review in a subsequent appeal.
The Court stated that the "interest of justice and fairplay" require the High Court, in cases with arguable points, to provide some indication of its reasoning for the dismissal.

In this specific case, the Court found it particularly inappropriate to dismiss the appellants' appeal while admitting the appeal of a co-accused, as the cases were interconnected and should have been considered together.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that when a High Court summarily dismisses a criminal appeal that raises serious and arguable points, it has a duty to provide reasons or some indication of its views. It held that it is improper for the High Court to dismiss such an appeal without giving an indication of its opinion on the points raised, as this is required by the interests of justice and fair play, and is necessary to assist the Supreme Court in any subsequent appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the appeal of four co-accused in limine, while simultaneously admitting the appeal of another co-accused in the same case, especially when the cases were interconnected.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's order was incorrect because it admitted the appeal of one co-accused (Kondu) while dismissing the appeal of the four appellants in the same case.
The cases were interconnected, and it was an eminently fit case for the appeals of all five accused to be considered together.
If the admitted appeal of the co-accused (Kondu) was successful, the case against the appellants would also require serious reconsideration.
The evidence on record needed to be scrutinized for all accused to determine how the appellants' case was distinguishable from the co-accused whose appeal was admitted.

To sustain the charge of rioting under s. 147 IPC, it was necessary to determine if an unlawful assembly was formed, which made it more appropriate to consider the case of all accused together on appeal.
respondent_arguments: The counsel for the State (respondent) made a 'faint attempt' to justify the High Court's order of dismissal.
The respondent ultimately conceded that the dismissal in limine of the appellants' appeal was 'insupportable' under the circumstances.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a High Court, when summarily dismissing a criminal appeal that raises serious and arguable points, has a duty to provide reasons or some indication of its views on the points raised.
appellant_arguments: The High Court should not have dismissed the appeal summarily as it raised arguable points that required consideration.
Summary dismissal is only justified in cases that prima facie raise no arguable issue.
In arguable cases, the High Court should provide some indication of its views on the points raised in its summary rejection order.
Providing reasons is necessary so that the Supreme Court, when hearing a special leave petition, has the benefit of the High Court's opinion and is not 'embarrassed' by its absence.
respondent_arguments: The text does not contain any specific arguments from the respondent on this issue.

cases.case_name: Mushtak Hussein v. The State of Bombay
cases.principle: It is improper for a High Court to summarily dismiss an appeal that raises arguable points without giving some indication of its views.

cases.case_name: Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli v. The State of Bombay
cases.principle: It is improper for a High Court to summarily dismiss an appeal that raises arguable points without giving some indication of its views.

cases.case_name: Chittaranjan Das v. State of West Bengal
cases.principle: It is improper for a High Court to summarily dismiss an appeal that raises arguable points without giving some indication of its views.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When an appeal in the High Court raises a serious and substantial point which is prima facie arguable, it is improper for that court to dismiss it summarily. Where an appeal by a co-accused from the same judgment is admitted, it is inappropriate to summarily dismiss the appeals of the other co-accused if their cases are interconnected, as this indicates the presence of arguable points requiring joint consideration.
obiter: In arguable cases that are summarily rejected, the High Court should give some indication of its views on the points raised so that the Supreme Court has the benefit of that opinion in the event of a special leave petition.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's order dismissing the appellants' appeal in limine was insupportable. It was improper to dismiss the appeal of four co-accused while simultaneously admitting the appeal of another co-accused in an interconnected case where the charge of rioting required considering all accused together. Furthermore, when a criminal appeal raises serious and arguable points, it is improper for a High Court to dismiss it summarily without giving some indication of its views on the points raised.
legal_tests_applied: Whether an appeal raises a serious and substantial point which is prima facie arguable, thus making it improper for a court to dismiss it summarily without giving reasons.
policy_considerations: The interest of justice and fairplay require the High Court in arguable cases to give an indication of its views on the points argued.

When a High Court provides reasons for a summary rejection, the Supreme Court, in the event of an appeal, has the benefit of the High Court's opinion and is not 'embarrassed' by having to deal with the matters without it.
